end of which some mortal fevers seized them 
which lasted twenty-four hours and afterwards 
they swelled up and burst, full of worms. This 
wretched pestilence lasted some days and dimin- 
ished the people so much that a large part of the 
food supplies remained ungathered. They re- 
gained their strength again and enjoyed another 
good fifteen years, at the end of which the old 
passions were reawakened and all, following their 
commanders, took up arms and reached the point 
of fighting a cruel battle in which 150,000 men 
died. After this war they returned to peace and 
to rest for another twenty years, when another 
doleful pestilence came upon them, of some large 
pustules over the whole body which rotted them 
with a great stench in such a way that their flesh 
fell from them in pieces in four or five days; and 
the Spaniards knew of many who survived it. 
When this pestilence was over, in the sierras 
of Mani in the province of Tutulxiu the Indian, 
called Chilam Cambal, priest, pronounced the 
prophecy of the cross which has been spoken of 
before; and Don Juan Cocom, who was so named 
when he became Christian, descendant of the 
Cocoms, showed a little book which his grand- 
father left him, which survived from the Cocom 
they killed in Mayapan, in which a deer was 
painted, saying that he had said that when those 
great deer, which were cows, entered the land, 
the worship of their gods would be changed, 
which he had seen fulfilled in the entrance of the 
Spaniards and with them the cows. They found 
them then living together in pueblos in very 
civilized fashion, and they kept them clean, the 
weeds cleared away and fruit trees planted. In 
the middle of the places they had the pueblos and 
near them the houses of the lords and priests and 
important people, and further away those of the 
common people. And the public wells were in 
the plazas. This dwelling thus together was on 
account of the wars because of which they ran the 
risk of being captured, sold and sacrificed. But 
with the wars of the Spaniards they were scat- 
tered. And their discords had increased so much 
that for any little cause they fought, and on this 
account they had captains appointed in each 
pueblo whom they obeyed, who performed their 
office with the advice of the lord and the priests. 
And so they never had peace, especially when the 
cultivation was over, and their greatest desire was 
to seize important men to sacrifice, because the 
greater the quality of the victim, the more ac- 
ceptable the service they did to god seemed to 


217 


them. The number of people sacrificed was great. 
And this custom was introduced into Yucatan by 
the Mexicans, and thus they were much given to 
idolatry and for this reason subject to their priests 
and given to repudiation, drunkenness and other 
sins. And in spite of all this they had things 
worthy of praise. The people of Yucatan are of 
good stature, well made and robust, and all usu- 
ally bow-legged because in childhood their 
mothers carry them sitting astride their hips. 
Many were cross-eyed because they allowed their 
hair to grow over their eyebrows, and raising 
their eyes as the hair went dancing they came to 
be cross-eyed. They deliberately made their fore- 
heads and heads flat. ‘hey had their ears pierced 
with earrings and very torn from the sacrifices 
for the blood which they drew from them. Usu- 
ally they had good faces and not very dark. 
They do not grow beards and when children they 
burned their faces so that they would not grow. 
They wore their hair long like women and inter- 
woven they made a garland of it about the head 
and left a pigtail behind. They had mirrors in 
which they looked at themselves and the women 

did not use them. They were much accustomed to 

bathing themselves without any modesty. They 

have always been fond of good odors. They 

painted their faces and bodies, as has been said, 

for the sake of elegance. The principales wore a 

strip eight fingers broad which served them for 

breeches, giving it some turns around the waist 

so that one end hung down before and the other 

behind, with elegant feather work. They wore 

long mantas, and square, knotted on the shoulders. 

They wore sandals or alpargatas of deer hide. 

Now they wear shirts, wide breeches (zara- 

gielles), hats and cotton sandals (alpargatas), and 

they let their beards grow and have good ones 

except that they are harsh like horse hairs. 


Cuaprer IV. Which continues the noteworthy things 
of Yucatan. 

They tattoed (/abrar) their bodies and the more 
tattooed they were the more elegant and valiant 
they were considered. They were given to the 
vice of drunkenness in the banquets they made in 
the feasts of the gods, at weddings and other re- 
joicings and dances. And when they were drunk 
they killed each other, the houses were burned, 
they committed adultery and ravished women by 
force without respect of father to sons nor other 
relationship and without resistance, for the houses 
were without doors. The wine was of honey and 


218 


water together with a certain root of a tree. ‘The 
beautiful women gave them drink and upon giving 
the glass turned their faces away until they re- 
turned it empty. And the women, seeing them 
drunk, undertook to take them home in order to 
avoid scandals. 
They were accustomed to have players for the 
feasts, and they had their trappings for it; and 
they are accustomed to deride the jests that pass 
among the Spaniards and they perform them with 
good acting and witty elegance so that they cause 
laughter. They have small kettle-drums and a 
hollow kettle-drum with a hoarse sound (which 
they use in other regions of the Indies), long and 
thin trumpets of hollow sticks with long and 
twisted gourds at the end, whistles of deer 
bones, large conch-shells, reed flutes. ‘Taking out 
the flesh, they make another instrument from the 
whole turtle which has a sad sound. They dance 
little, and many at a time so that eight hundred 
take part in one dance, and although they dance 
all day they never fail to keep time. The men 
were accustomed to dance with the women in but 
few dances. When a quarrel took place they 
named judges as arbiters for satisfaction of the 
injury, and if, on account of the payment, the 
condemned man was forced to impoverish him- 
self, his relatives helped him. And today they are 
liberal and very generous and no one enters their 
houses whom they do not feed and the same 
happens on the road or wherever they go. Their 
counting is by fives up to twenty, by twenties to 
one hundred, and from there by four hundreds 
and then up to eight thousand, and then up to an 
infinite number. And they count on the ground or 
something flat. They were accustomed to be 
great boasters concerning their descent, on ac- 
count of which all were considered relatives and 
they helped each other a great deal. Women were 
not admitted to inheritances except through pity; 
and they left an additional bequest to him who 
had aided his father most notably in winning the 
property. When there were no male children the 
brothers inherited and the nearest relatives. When 
the heirs were very young they gave them the 
nearest relatives as guardians and they returned 
their property to them when they came of age, 
and not to do so was a very ugly thing. 
Formerly they used to get married at twenty 
years of age. Afterwards they married at twelve 
and fourteen, and since they did not love their 
wives they immediately had recourse to repudia- 
tion for any slight cause; and although they might 


APPENDIX A 


already be men and have sons, they returned to 
the wife without feeling uneasy in doing s0, 
although another might have had her, Bur if the 
women were not good while they were living 
with them they could not bear it with patience 
because they are very jealous, and they left them 
for this reason and had great quarrels and deaths 
on this account. They did not take as wife their 
step-mothers or sisters-in-law. They did not take 
a woman of their own name on the father’s side, 
which they considered bad. They contracted 
matrimony with all the other relatives on their 
mother’s side even though they were first cousins. 
The dowries consisted of dresses and things of 
little value. The greater part was spent on feasts. 
The feast having been prepared and the guests 
and the priest being present, the fathers-in-law 
summoned the couple. A speech was made with 
regard to how that marriage had been discussed 
and considered and how it was arranged. After 
the speech was made the priest perfumed the 
house and blessed the bridal pair with prayers 
and they remained married. And the sons-in-law 
served the fathers-in-law four or five years and 
helped them a great deal, if not, they threw them 
out and gave their daughters to others, from which 
great scandals arose. The widowers and those 
already men made their own arrangements to get 
married without the formality of [using] friends. 
In all the provinces of New Spain baptism has 
been found in Yucatan alone, and in their tongue 
it means “‘to be born again.’’ They held it in 
such great devotion and reverence that no one 
failed to receive it. They thought they received 
in it a pure disposition to be good and not to be 
harmed by the demons and to attain glory, which 
they hoped for. It was given them between the 
ages of three and twelve and no one was married 
without it. They chose for it a day which should 
not be unfortunate. The fathers fasted for three 
days beforehand and abstained from their wives. 
The priests took care of the purification of the 
dwelling, casting out the demon with certain cere- 
monies. When these were over the children went 
one by one and the priest threw a little maize and 
ground incense into their hands and they threw 
it into a brazier. And they sent wine out of the 
pueblo in a vessel, with orders to the Indian not 
to drink it nor look back, and by this means they 
thought they had driven out the demon. The priest 
came forth clad in long and heavy vestments and 
with a hyssop in his hand. He put white cloths 
on the children’s heads, asked the older ones 


HERRERA 219 


whether they had committed any sin and when 
they confessed he took them aside and blessed 
them with prayers, sprinkling them with the 
hyssop, and with a certain water which they kept 
in a bone he annointed their foreheads and the 
features of the face and between the digits of the 
feet and hands. And then the priest arose and took 
the cloths off the children, and, certain presents 
having been made, they remained baptized and 
the feast ended with banquets. And in addition to 
the three days the father had to abstain from his 
wife nine more. 

‘The afflictions and troubles which happened to 
this people, they were aware that they came upon 
them on account of their sins, and in order to 
escape them they made use of confession in their 
illnesses and in any danger of death, as well as in 
childbirth or similar things. They declared their 
sins publicly, and if they were forgetful their re- 
latives reminded them, if the priest was there, to 
him, and if not, to their fathers and mothers and 
wives to their husbands. They accused themselves 
of theft, homicide, the sin of the flesh, false wit- 
ness; and if they did not die plenty of dissensions 
arose between husbands and wives. They did not 
confess sins of intention although they considered 
them bad. It was permissible for the lords to 
enjoy the use of their female slaves. They were 
great fasters and much given to prayer, with dif- 
ferent prayers which they had for their times, 
and besides the public temples, many had orato- 
ries in their houses; but what they venerated most 
were the temples of the island of Cozumel and 
the well of Chichen, which were as Rome and 
Jerusalem are among us, where they went on 
pilgrimage, and those who had been there were 
considered sanctified; and those who did not go 
sent their offerings. And there were some idols 
that gave replies. In other places the priests in- 
vented them, deceiving the people in order to get 
the presents from them. And these wizards per- 
formed the office of physicians and cured with 
herbs, blood-lettings, incensings and words of the 
devil. And the office of opening the breasts of the 

sacrificial victims, which was esteemed in Mexico, 
carried little honor here. In Yucatan they sacri- 
ficed with festivals and dances, asking the gods 
for mercy on account of some ill they had. Some- 
times they shot the victim with arrows, aiming 
at his heart, he being tied to a pole, and after- 
wards they took him to the place of sacrifice to 
open him and take out his heart. And these un- 
derstood that they were going to heaven. Then 


they threw them down the steps. They flayed 
them, the priest put on the skin and danced, and 
they buried the body in the patio of the temple; 
and sometimes they were eaten, although those 
of Yucatan were not such great eaters of human 
flesh. 

For these sacrifices they captured slaves in 
wars and condemned many of their own people 
as such for some crimes, and when these were 
lacking they were so devout that they gave their 
little nephews and even their sons. Those who 
captured slaves in war were considered as valiant 
men when they returned, for their wars did not 
last very long. They spent many days in banquets 
telling of their prowess because they were vain 
of valor, and in the time of their bringing-up, 
besides the respect which they taught them to 
have for the old and advanced in age and for 
working and being virtuous, they turned their 
inclination infinitely toward war, which, as has 
been said, lasted but a short time on account of 
the small food provision which the women could 
carry on their backs for lack of beasts of burden. 
And thus they finished them quickly, soon coming 
to blows. The women of Yucatan are, on the one 
hand, of better appearance than the Spanish 
women, and they are well made and not homely 
usually, and those who are beautiful take much 
pride in it. They are not white but of a yellowish 
brown color caused by the sun and bathing them- 
selves. They make fun of the Spanish women for 
the care they take of their faces. They filed their 
teeth, pierced the cartilage of their nostrils and 
placed there as an ornament an amber stone. They 
put earrings in their ears and tattooed their bodies 
from the waist up, except their breasts for nurs- 
ing. They often bathed in cold water like the men 
with little modesty. Some of them stained them- 
selves with red like the men and put liquid ambar 
in that ointment and remained very pretty and 
sweet smelling, and it lasted many days. They 
wear their hair very long and parted; they dress 
their hair prettily, that of the married women 
different from that of the maidens. They wore a 
dress like a sack, long and wide, open on both 
sides and sewn as far as the hips; and they had 
good bodies. They also got drunk in the feasts, 
although they ate by themselves. ‘Those who lack 
them have a great desire for sons. They are pru- 
dent, courteous and sociable; they are not very 
secretive. They are not very clean in their per- 
sons nor in their houses in spite of all their wash- 
ing. They were devout and religious and they did

not shed blood for the demons and they did not 
allow them to go to the sacrifices in the temples 
except on a certain festival which certain old 
women attended. 

They had an excessive fear of death; they 
mourned their dead greatly, by day in silence and 
by night with doleful cries. They continued sad 
for many days. They made fasts for the dead. 
They shrouded him, filling his mouth with ground 
maize so that he should not lack food in the other 
life. They buried them in their houses or at the 
back of them, throwing the idols into the grave, 
and if he was a priest, his books. Upon burying 
the deceased they abandoned the house for fear 
of death. They burned the bodies of the lords 
and they put the ashes in great vessels and built 
temples over them. They made statues of wood 
to their fathers, and, leaving the back of the head 
hollow, they put the ashes there and kept the 
statues among the idols with great reverence. 
Ancient graves of many kinds have been found. 
In the pueblo of Mani, opening a grave enclosed 
in living rock on all sides, a body was found in it 
of extremely large size, destroyed except for 
some pieces of the thigh bones of the legs. And 
they took out of the head a tooth which weighed 
little less than a pound and a half. And there is a 
belief that anciently there were men of very 
great stature in this land. Those of Yucatan have 
gone beyond the other nations of the Indies in the 
belief in the immortality of the soul, because they 
have always believed that after this mortal life 
there was another more excellent one which the 
soul was going to enjoy when separated from the 


body. They said that the future life was divided 
into good and bad, the latter for the vicious, the 
good, for the good; and they believed that this 
was a delightful place for living without trouble, 
with abundance of food and sweet drink, under a 
tree of great shade beneath which they were to 
rest; and that the bad life was in a lower place, 
suffering great necessities of hunger, cold, sad- 
ness and torments. And they did not give an 
account of who had taught them this their heaven 
and hell. 

And to finish these things about Yucatan, the 
sun is not hidden nor does it go so far from this 
land that the nights ever come to be longer than 
the days, and when they are longest they are 
usually equal. From San Andres to Santa Lucia, 
when they begin to increase, they regulated 
themselves by night, in order to know the hour, 
by the morning star and the Pleiades and Gemini, 
by day, by midday, and from north to south they 
have given names to sections, by means of which 
they understood each other and regulated them- 
selves. They had their perfect year like ours of 
three hundred and sixty-five days, and of these 
the year had twelve months and five days and 
six hours. They call these months V, which 
means moon, and they counted it from the time 
it came out new until it did not appear. They also 
counted the year of eighteen months, each month 
of twenty days, according to the Mexican custom, 
and they had their twenty characters with which 
they named them, omitting to give a name to the 
five days and six hours which are extra in this 
reckoning as they considered them unfortunate.

Cuapter XX. Concerning the false religion and idolatry 
of the Occidental Indians and their abominable and 
savage use and custom of eating human flesh and of 
hunting and killing one another for this purpose, and 
concerning their bloody and horrible sacrifices in which 
they killed and sacrified men to their gods. 


HERE God is not and does not dwell, all 

good is lacking and all reason and justice, 
and the ultimate and the peak of all the evils 
which can befall a nation and people is to lack 
knowledge of the true God and to be separated 
from Him. The emulator of the works of God 
and the father of error and the origin and root of 
all evil, the devil, just as he applied all his study 
and care to separating man from the way of God 
and deceiving and blinding all the peoples with 
false religions, determined to do the same here in 
times past and did so among those wretched peo- 
ples of the Indies, involving all of them, without 
excepting any nation, in a thousand kinds of 
abominable idolatries, in which state they con- 
tinued and were from their establishment until 
they were found and discovered by the Spaniards 
(which is absolutely certain and true), for all 
those of the islands were idolaters, the Mexicans 
and Guatemalans and all their neighbors, idola- 
ters, and the Peruvians and all the other inhabit- 
ants of the Indies, idolaters too. The secret of 
this mystery and the reason why the sun of the 
Christian religion and of the true belief in the 
true God dawned so late for them, God Himself 
is the knower of it and we reserve and remit the 
solution of this question and doubt to Him alone, 
as we have said on other occasions. 

The island Indians worshipped the devil and 
were extremely subject to him on account of the 
great threats he made and the awful apparitions 
in which he appeared to them, as well as the 
Mexicans, Guatemalans, Yucatecans and the 
others in their vicinity. The Peruvians held the 
sun as God and gave the honor and worship due 
to God their Maker to the creature. In the New 
Kingdom was the flower of all the superstition 
and idolatry, and please God it may not be so 
today, where it is and was very usual for the

priests and mohanes to consult the demon and 
for him to appear to them and their seeing him in 
various figures and forms which he took for the 
purpose, and speaking to them and replying to 
their questions and queries; and it went this far 
and this was the sum total of that false religion 
of all the Indies. Although those of the islands 
did not have their sacrifices nor so regular a 
priesthood as in other regions, the demon moved 
them with great supersition and auguries and 
with other similar inventions of his. 

In Mexico and Yucatan and Guatemala and in 
all those provinces in that region idolatry was 
prevalent in the highest degree and the devil was 
served very much to the cost of those peoples. 
The temples they had were sumptuous with a 
great number of priests for their cult. In all Mex- 
ico and in those neighboring provinces there were 
sacrifices, not only of gold and silver and of the 
fruits which they gathered and possessions they 
had, but even of living men, whom they killed 
in great numbers, and very often of blood which 
the men drew from their own members. 

In Mexico and Guatemala and Yucatan and in 
all those provinces, they had, in addition to their 
temples, some very high edifices, dedicated and 
designed especially for the sacrifice of men, in 
the form of square pyramids which were very 
broad at the foundation and base and narrowed 
by degrees toward the top until there remained 
at the summit a crest or small square, which 
could accommodate a half dozen or a dozen men, 
and in the middle of it a pile of stones was erected, 
prolonged and sharp and tapered at the top. And 
they called this whole building cu in the Mexican 
language. And they took up there the unfortunate 
man whom they were going to sacrifice and the 
priest laid him naked across that pile of stone 
which we mentioned supine and face up. When 
he had been placed thus the priest of the master 
of that ceremony approached and with an ex- 
tremely sharp flint, because they had no other 
knives there, he opened him with all the quickness 
in the world on the side of the heart and tore it 
out and threw it on high, offering it to their gods; 
all this, as I have said, with so much ease and skill 
that his quickness was an extraordinary thing.

And this kind of sacrifice was very usual and 
ordinary, although the killing of men as a sacri- 
fice was done in two ways, because some were 
offered and sacrificed of their own free will while 
others were forced. The first were inhabitants 
and natives of the pueblos where they were 
sacrificed. Those compelled were captives and 
men taken in the wars they made against other 
pueblos, whom they kept in prisons and in cages 
for this purpose, fattening them. 

Those who were sacrificed by their own free 
will were few. Some did it in time of necessity 
and on account of their pride and vainglory in 
order to leave that memory of themselves; and 
for that reason not only was the memory of those 
who thus killed themselves perpetually celebrated 
but those of that lineage were highly esteemed. 
The day when one of those sacrifices was offered 
was celebrated greatly and one of the most im- 
portant and holy spectacles they thought they had. 
There was a special place for this and it was per- 
formed with much pomp and solemnity. In the 
first place the sacrificial victim offered himself 
to the priests and made manifest to them his in- 
tention and vow, and the day on which it was to 
take place having been designated, the unfortunate 
wretch ascended to that place, which was very 
high, and, the people having gathered to see so 
sad a spectacle, he made an oration in which he 
gave an account of his motive and intention and 
he praised that kind of sacrifice and started to 
tell of all those of his lineage who had offered 
themselves in that way, and speaking and reaching 
the point of counting himself among the number 
of the others, he threw himself down there below, 
dashing himself to pieces, the people at once has- 
tening with great devotion to take a piece of that 
flesh in order to eat it, as a thing they held in 
great devotion and veneration. The other sacri- 
fices of men captured and compelled to it by force 
were sO many in number, especially in Mexico, 
that each year, it is painful to state, some Indians 
affirm that more than fifty thousand were killed 
each year. And those who were present at the 
taking of Mexico say that the sacrifice was so 

great and continuous in those days when the 
Indians were besieged and most hemmed in in 
Mexico that when Hernando Cortés and the 
Spaniards took the city, going to Tateluleo, which 
was their principal temple, they were unable to 
enter a retired room where the sacrifice was per- 
formed on account of rhe great amount of human 
blood they found shed there, for the captives were 


killed and sacrificed by others forced co it and 
inhabitants and natives and those who offered 
themselves of their own free will killed them 
selves with their own hand. 

The sacrificed bodies of those captives and 
prisoners were not left useless and to no purpose, 
because after what concerned their religion had 
been fulfilled, their flesh was w erghed and sold 
publicly for human sustenance as if they were 
sheep or pigs or other animals, for it is meat they 
crave and they ate it with great pleasure. And 
in addition to the flesh of these sacrifices, every- 
one who had slaves that he had taken in various 
wars killed the one he wished of them when he 
had a fancy to do so, and in this way also many 
died. 

In addition to these extraordinary sacrifices it 
was very usual, as I have already said, among the 
Mexicans and Guatemalans (for all had certain 
sacrifices and rites) to sacrifice to the idols that 
they found on the roads, anointing the face of the 
idol with blood they drew right there, either from 
their ears, piercing them, or from their nostrils 
or tongue, and even from their private parts, ac- 
cording to what others say, so that anyone who 
passed by any idol and did not offer him any por- 
tion of blood drawn there from his own body was 
not considered devout or good, in the same way 
that we do reverence when we come upon any 
cross or image on any journey, for thus that blind 
people likewise had their shrines and sanctuaries 
in the fields and roads. 

The Mexicans and Guatemalans had a great 
number of priests in those temples and their per- 
petual abode and dwelling was there, where they 
practiced such abominable lusts and sins that it 
is an abominable and disgraceful thing to describe; 
and those men had already acquired so many 
rights, or more properly speaking, introduced 
such nefarious and widespread customs in this 
case among the people, that in order not to offend 
chaste ears it is necessary to pass over them in 
silence. In addition to the cult of the temple and 
othce of the sacrifices, these priests served in 
consulting the demon about wars which the lord 
wished to undertake or about other public affairs 
or those concerming the lords. And for this pur- 
pose those deceivers and ministers of the devil 
had their pacts and agreements with him and their 
particular rites and ceremonies for this alone. 
And they consulted him at certain hours and by 
night and with barbarous and outlandish words 
which the people did not understand, language

In the provinces of Yucatan, although they

Among other sacrifices which the devil had 
taught them in those provinces of Yucatan was 
one of which they made use in time of necessity, 
and when they were in need of rain for their 
maize, which sacrifice they made with the death 
and offering of one or two Indian virgins or the

lords was and where the priests were and the

they all went in procession with her by a paved

a large and deep cenote which was there, of the

a shrine which was near there, where the priests 
withdrew with her. And they instructed her and 
informed her concerning what she was to ask

brought her forth from there, and having tied 
her with a long rope, they lowered her down to

While I was in that province during my inspec-

going to kill her. And the boldness and assurance 
of that virgin in her speech had so great an effect 
that they left her and sacrificed another in her 
place. 

The Yucatecans had a certain other sacrifice 
of fire, which, on a certain day of the year and 
in places by night, they made and celebrated after 
having eaten and drunk copiously, because in 
such times the devil makes his gains. And they 
arranged it in this fashion. A large quantity of 
very dry wood ready to be burned was brought, 
and when it had been gathered and collected in a 
certain place which they had already set aside 
for this purpose, the priests encircled it, and first 
they performed certain ceremonies and set fire 
to it, and while the fire lasted and all the wood 
was being consumed the uproar of the people 
went on and the drinking and getting drunk. And 
the priests invoked the devil and made their pacts 
with him in the meantime. When the wood had 
already been burned up and all had become live 
coals, they levelled that terrible fire with long

In Nicaragua, for let us finish with what con- 
cerns the district and area toward Mexico, they 
also had, in addition to the general idolatry of

With regard to the Peruvian Indians, there also 
existed great devoutness and superstition, and a 
large number of priests in their temples, which 
they called in their language houses of the sun, 
which they worshipped and venerated especially. 
There were also in those temples of theirs and 
houses of the sun a large number of maidens and 
virgins who were dedicated there with a vow of 
perpetual virginity and continence, like the Vestal 
Virgins of the Romans, whom they kept well 
guarded, and they punished with terrible penal- 
ties those who were found with any one of them 
and the penalty for the maidens was also death.

Among the other duties of those priests, most im-

to atise in the morning and to place their table 
of many vessels of silver and gold and to fill them 
with that chicha of theirs and drink and food so 
that when the sun rose and appeared over the

“mocha” which they used as a salutation, and

the Spaniards. They had great riches in those

from Peru. 
In the New Kingdom likewise idolatry was 
very active and although it was not practiced

$0 many men as in Mexico, with all that it was

Kingdom would go, and those who are not Chris- 
tians go now, night and day and for a whole 
year, working naked and unshod and dying with

he earned and earns, and the eagerness of those

And this is the reason why much gold is found in

there and they have as cager desires for finding it

The Indians of the New Kingdom had another 
kind of sacrifice peculiar to them, and it Was, in 
time of need, to shoot with arrows some children 
whom they had taken and seized fromm their ne- 
mics and opponents in their wars, placing than 
on high poles, tying them there and shooting

In some parts of the Indies, although with a 
mixture of many errors, they had knowledge 
and remembrance of the general flood and they 
confessed that there was another world and age

the soul, barbarously and in a confused fashion

finished their days miserably, remaining there

to the sacrifices and idolatries of the Occidental

There also existed among the Occidental] In- 
dians their kind of oral confession of sins, I 
mean of those sins that were considered such by 
those peoples, such as homicide, theft and adul- 
tery, etc., although it was not uniform nor of the 
same kind in all regions. The Yucatecan Indians 
had the custom of confessing themselves once in 
their lives, and this when they felt they were so 
near to death that they could not escape, and they 
made this confession of theirs in public and before 
anyone who wished to hear it, telling the whole 
course of their lives and telling there their public 
and private guilts, and sometimes many troubles 
and dissensions arose from this, especially from

the confessions of the women with regard to their 
husbands, if it happened that they escaped and 
survived their illness, so that in all ways that 
infernal spirit, either all at once or by degrees, 
always managed to make trouble among those 
poor peoples. 

Among the Utlatecan and Guatemalan Indians 
the confession was made in an extreme fashion 
and more frequently, and every time that many 
sins were known to exist in the public and their 
idols and false gods were angry on account of 
them, the whole pueblo gathered in observation 
of this ceremony and they sought among them an 
old woman, the most decrepit and advanced in 
years they could find, and they took her out into 
the country, the whole town accompanying her, 
and they looked for a cross-road or meeting place 
of many roads and seated her there, and hemmed 
in and surrounded by all, in loud voices and all 
at once each one confessed and publicly told his 
sins and guilts. And when that shouted and 
tumultuous confession was finished the priest 
drew near with a great stone and struck the poor 
old woman so many blows on the head that he 
killed her, and when she was dead the whole 
town and all the confessants approached and 
covered her with stone in a moment, erecting and 
raising over her a great tomb, and with this the 
sacrifice and confession came to an end and they 
returned to their houses completely convinced 
that now all their sins were taken away and that 
the town remained purified and clean on account 
of that sacrifice and the poor old woman bore the 
sins of all on her shoulders to represent them 
there to their gods to appease their anger. And 
this was the kind of confession of those Indians, 
which, carefully considered, seems to bear some 
resemblance to that sacrifice and confession 
which is mentioned and discussed in chapter 16 
of Leviticus, which under the old law was made 
to the scapegoat. 

There are not lacking those who put the ques- 
tion whether oral confession has some natural 
origin and instigation; and what we have said 
with regard to the confession of those Indians 
seems to be in favor of this, for without knowl- 
edge of any divine precept, living in accordance 
with natural law, they had the use and custom of 
confessing their guilts and sins as we have said. 
Nevertheless, although penitence and repentance 
for sin and for the evil done may be natural, 
publishing it and making it known seems rather 
to oppose natural law than to have origin in it, or

and malice on the method and medicine which is 
given them for its cure since they are unwilling 
to make good use of the healthful remedy. 

There was also practiced and used among the 
Yucatecan Indians a certain kind of baptism 
which, although it was not obligatory nor gen- 
eral among all, was held in repute in that false 
religion of theirs as a thing of great sanctity and 
peculiar merit in those who wished to abide by 
it and use it. Its ceremony from beginning to end 
was in the following manner: 

Before all things the boy or girl who was to be 
baptized was destined by the parents for it as 
soon as it was born, and they offered it for that 
act and placed upon its head a certain insignia by 
which it was distinguished from the others and it 
was understood that that baby was destined for 
baptism. And when they had already attained to 
six or seven years, the time when they were to 
be baptized was discussed with the priest, and 
the day having been appointed, they prepared the 
house of the priest or the place where it was to 
take place with branches and many other foliages 
and they gathered all the boys and girls who were 
to be found in the pueblo destined for baptism. 
They took them as in procession to the said 
place, the boys on their side being preceded by an 
old man as godfather, and the girls on the other 
side with an old and aged woman. And when they 
reached the priest he received them with great 
approbation and proceeding in their ceremonies 
rites he first took from the boys and girls those 
Insignia we have mentioned, which they had 
worn up to that time, and after other observances 
and ceremonies he laved their heads and with this 
they remained baptized and they were always 
considered more devout and sanctified. By this 


TOMAS LOPEZ MEDEL a | 


and other similar ceremonies which have been 
observed in the Yucatecan Indians and in others, 
some of our Spaniards have taken occasion to 
persuade themselves and believe that in times 
past some of the apostles or a successor to them 
passed over to the West Indies and that ulti- 
timately those Indians were preached to. I con- 
sider it a fabulous thing and without any base of 
truth for the reasons I brought forward in an- 
other place, and what these persons say is not a 
likely thing because if those whom they say went 
from these regions here by water they would 
have had to embark and it was impossible for a 
certain number of ships not to have gone, and if 
so, we would have had some mention of it by 
writers of the past, and we would also have had 
knowledge of it from the Indies, because to think 
that they went by land is an impossible thing. 
And the said ceremonies must not move us be- 
cause all could be work of the devil and taken and 
placed there by his dispensation, for he is ac- 
customed to steal like a monkey that prophecied 
by Christ and dedicated for the particular wor- 
ship of God with a mixture of many errors and 
impose it as law among his worshippers and 
adorers. Let he who wishes authority for this 
see Justin Martyr in the admonition Ad gente. 

I shall not omit to describe here a praiseworthy 
custom of the Guatemalan and Utlatecan Indians 
which occurs to me now. These Indians were so 
nobly zealous and lovers of the public welfare 
that they loved and honored the magistrates and 
administrators of the republic who with most zeal 
and notable works promoted their republic and 
watched for the public good, and when they died 
they buried them in the houses of their cabildos 
and ayuntamientos in that very spot where they 
were accustomed to sit and to administer justice 
and to vote and execute those notable works 
which they did in the republic. This was the most 
sovereign glory which could be given to a man 
among them. And in this manner by honoring the 
dead they aroused the living for other such and 
greater works. Would to God that in these de- 
praved times, where the pernicious inclination to 
private interest does so much harm, we might 
find some similar medicine in order to uproot it 
and remove it from the hearts of men. 

The custom of eating human flesh was so in- 
grained and accepted among those barbarian 
peoples that in very many parts and regions the 
nefarious custom of killing men described was 
not to make a sacrifice and oblation of them to 


their gods as the Mexicans and Guatemalans and 
many others did it, but purely and solely for this 
end of satisfying and feeding their appetite for 
eating human flesh and having it for their sus- 
tenance. (In the margin): A line has been cut at 
the end of folio 77. Some of these people de- 
praved in this respect, when they were unable to 
hunt and kill other men secretly and by stealth, 
did it openly and shamelessly and do it, those 
tainted by this vice going armed and on the point 
of war to other regions to make their attacks and 
wage war on them like one who goes to a boar 
hunt or for other game, and this was even the 
most usual thing. 

In this account enter all the provinces of 
Brazil, which is a very extensive and long thing, 
together with many others which extend toward 
the Marafion river and Venezuela, and some 
islands of Caribe Indians, who are so called be- 
cause they eat human flesh. The practice and 
continual exercise of all these is that from time 
to time many of them see fit to join in a squadron 
and go armed and on the point of war to other 
provinces of other tame Indians who are not 
tainted by that evil custom and to seize all they 
can of them for their food and sustenance, those 
who kill them eating them on the spot, and those 
who take them alive bringing them to their lands 
in order to eat them like the rest in their feasts 
and banquets and ordinary meals. It is said that 
the dissolution of the Brazilian Indians is so 
great that it happens that when three or four in- 
habitants go to the forests for wood or to some 
other place and one or two of them are missing, 
it is because the others who were stronger ate 
them. This is a daily occurrence among them. 

We may number with these all the Panche 
Indians, because although they may not be so 
bellicose and cruel as the Caribes in the desire 
and appetite for eating human flesh, in eating it 
when they have it and can get it I do not believe 
they have any advantage over them. The Panche 
Indians are a well built and proportioned people 
and very artless and simple, if this bad custom 
were to be uprooted and taken from them. This 
nation of the Panches is settled and spread 
through all the rapids and shores of the Rio 
Grande de la Magdalena on one side and on the 
other from the river called Vélez up toward the 
east to Neiba, which is all hot country, in such a 
way that the Panches extend up that river for 
150 leagues and even more. I say this counting 
the Muso Indians with them and also the Colima

[ndians, whom | consider Panches in their con- 
dition and way of living. 

There also enter into this account and number- 
ing of the nefarious custom of eating human 
flesh all the provinces of Popayan from the 
boundaries of Pasto to Santa Fe and Antioquia, 
the whole extending to the South Sea, and all 
that which lies between the two rivers of Cauca 
and the Magdalena, of which we spoke at length 
in other chapters. In all of these provinces there 
has been and in many there still exists so much 
evil that I believe it has been one of the most de- 
praved of the Indies, and we could tell of them 
very cruel deeds in the case and matter concern- 
ing which we are speaking. 

On the shore of the Magdalena river in the 
direction of the city of Popayan, on a slope about 
a league or two from the river is settled a little 
province of Indians who are called the Pisaos, 
of whom it is said that they have no other agri- 
culture nor labor except going to catch fish, and, 
the most usual, to hunt men, crossing the river 
to some provinces of Indians named the Zuazos, 
tame and simple, who are settled toward the 
other slope, opposite, toward the north of that 
valley through which the great river passes. And 
these Pisaos have done and do so much carnage 
among them that it is a lamentable thing to tell the 
amount they tell of them, for certainly they have 
laid waste and depopulated those provinces of the 
Zuazo Indians. When I arrived in the Villa of 
Neiba certain Spaniards told me that a cacique or 
captain of those Pisaos being a prisoner, a cacique 
of the Zuazo Indians learning of it went to the 
prison where the other was prisoner, and they say 

that in the presence of many Spaniards he took 
out a long cord he had brought, full of knots, say- 
ing in his language to him who was prisoner, 
“Look, evil man, you have eaten of my people as 
many Indians as there are knots and you have 
left only me. Eat me, eat me, and you will finish 
all 

In another province near there which the 
Spaniards call the Culata de Timana, there are 
some warlike Caribe Indians concerning whom | 
was told that a few days before I arrived in 
Timana, they had come to make an attack on the 
peaceful Indians, and they did it in such a way 
that before assistance could be sent, they took 
away more than seventy loads of the dead, which 
the Spaniards forced them to abandon, although 
they arrived too late. 


In ‘Timana there also occurred a case related 


by many of an Indian who was eaten whole by 
another Indian, although he threw him up later. 
The most reverent bishop of Chiapa tells it in 
his writings. 

These cruelties were so advanced among some 
of these Indians that not only did they practice 
them and commit them with strangers and foreign- 
ers but even with their own subjects and natives 
and with their inhabitants and neighbors. It is told 
by many that during the conquest of Popayan cer- 
tain Spaniards met in the field a cacique of that coun- 
try who was bringing with him another Indian 
loaded with the hands and feet of men whom they 
had killed. And when those Spaniards reproved 
so great a cruelty and excess, the cacique replied 
to them asking what it mattered to them, for they 
ate their own Indians not those of others, as if 
one should say, “If you think you have license 
and freedom to eat your own herds and eat what 
you see fit, I also intend to have and use it to kill 
and eat my Indians.”’ 

In the district of the provinces of Arma, 
Antioquia and Santa Fe there was no security in 
this regard among the very inhabitants, because 
working together or travelling by some road or 
in any other place, when one became careless the 
other turned on him and killed him in order to eat 
him, and they even tell (if it is a thing worth be- 
lieving) that they ate their own sons, especially 
the children of their slave women, whom they 
bought for this purpose alone, and when they 
felt like it they also went after the mother. 

By these errors then, and by these idolatries 
and false religions and by these horrible and 
savage customs, that perverse Satan, ancient 
enemy of man, conducted and trained those 
wretched peoples of the Indies and kept them in 
this miserable state for many centuries until the 
mercy of their Creator and Maker saw fit to 
communicate to them His grace and gospel, on 
which account much of this has ceased and 
through the goodness of God will cease entirely 
(if we do not impede the divine hand of God) . This 
has been told not through hatred for those poor 
peoples, for whom we desire the benevolence of 
all the men of the world, but in order that the 
labors of the devil may be seen and in order that 
we may understand the wretchedness and mis- 
fortune to which a miserable man may come when 
separated from God or lacking Him, so that 
there is no reason for us to vaunt ourselves and 
arise with spirit of hate and ill will against the 
poor Indians, with the memory of their idolatries 


TOMAS LOPEZ MEDEL 


and errors. Rather we are obliged to take pity on 
them and procure for them the road and remedy 
for their salvation. 

If the vanity and lightness of those Romans and 
Athenians and of many other nations where so 
many philosophers abounded and the knowledge 
of the world was so strong reached so far in 
abominable idolatries and false religions that, as 
is quoted by the glorious Augustine in the book 
of Civitate Dei in many places, and by Eusebius 
in the fifth book of the Preparatione Evangelica 
referring to Hesiod, a sage of the most ancient of 
those peoples, they came to so great madness and 
dementia that more than forty thousand gods 
existed among them, with so much superstition 
that for every little thing and for every human 
act, however little and unworthy it might be, 
they had a particular god dedicated to it, it is no 
great thing that in comparison with the number 
of those so wise and great philosophers the idol- 
atry and false religion of those western people 
passes and is overlooked, so uncultured and bar- 
barian that in many regions they did not even 
know the principles of natural law. 

Then, with regard to the abominable custom 
which the Occidental Indians had of sacrificing 
men to their gods, if anyone should wish to seize 
upon it in order to hate them, let him consider 
that this abomination was much used among 
those ancient peoples of this world and by the 
devil’s luck he took it from here to transfer it 
to the Indies. 

Eusebio, in the fourth book of the treatise 
cited above, abominates and cites a thousand 
evils against the blindness of the ‘‘Rodos”’ 
(inhabitants of Rhodes?) who sacrificed men to 
their gods, and tells there that those whom they 
were to sacrifice got drunk first with much wine 
in order that they might not feel the pain and 
suffering of so severe a fate, which is also the 
custom among the Indians, which indicates that 
the devil took that abominable custom and kind 
of sacrifice from here and carried it to the Indies 
in the way that malign spirit is accustomed to 
change and transfer evil customs from one part 

to another for his infernal purposes and ends, God 
allowing it in accordance with his hidden judg- 
ments. That said author also tells that in many 
other regions of this world in the time of that 
past paganism, the sacrifice of men to their false 


Pati 


gods was much in use and practice. And it is a 
thing well-known and mentioned by many au- 
thors that ancient Saturn demanded the tenth part 
of all the men and women born for his sacrifice 
alone, so that by pact and agreement the yearly 
sacrifice came to be three men in the squadron 
each day, so that by these wise men and in that 
antiquity of this world there must have occurred 
likewise the shedding of as much human blood as 
was shed by those barbarian nations of the Indies 
each year as a sacrifice to their gods. Therefore 
the Occidental Indians did not have anything in 
this respect which had not been seen here and 
was more abominable and bloody, although the 
practice and abominable custom of the others of 
killing men solely on account of their appetite 
for eating human flesh is worthy of instantaneous 
and rigorous remedy. 

Eusebius the Alexandrian in the book of 
Demostratione Evangelica says that the supreme 
mercy and goodness of God thought well to take 
pity on men by sending them the remedy for 
their redemption and the Author of it, His only 
Son, at the time when the world was most 
foolish and had already come to greater and more 
abominable sins and evils with its blindness; and 
one of the greatest evils and sins which that 
author tells there, to which men had come and 
their malice had brought them, was that fathers 
married their daughters, and brothers their sis- 
ters, and that men considered human flesh a 
delicacy, killing each other in order to eat it; and 
this he sets down as the greatest viciousness of 
the past world here. And in accordance with this 
we may weep for the wretchedness of the Occi- 
dental Indians and for their consummate malice, 
and we can say the same of them, that God 
wished to take pity on them and send them the 
remedy. His divine goodness allowing the Indies 
to be found and discovered so that they might 
deserve to be evangelized and brought to the wor- 
ship of their true God at the time when their 
faults and sins had reached these extremes de- 
scribed. 

May the divine goodness of our God not desire 
the death of men but their conversion and may 
the discovery of those wretched peoples have 
been in order that in all regions they may be fully 
evangelized and saved from their abominations 
and errors, for the great service of God. Amen.
