APPENDIX D 


Cervantes de Salazar, Crénica de la Nueva Espana Libro Segundo, 
Caps. XX V-XXIX (pp. 110-122). 


CHAPTER XXV. How in Cozumel Cortes had information 
concerning Jerénimo de Aguilar. 


Co being in this situation, and the trade 
and friendship between his men and the In- 
dians of Cozumel ever increasing, he had news 
that inland on the coast of Yucatan there were 
five or six Spaniards, whom the Indians of 
Cozumel described by signs, saying that they 
were men resembling ours, and, touching their 
own beards, they signified that those of those 
men were long and full. Understanding that they 
were Spaniards, Cortes was seized by a strong 
desire to know more of them; but since it was 
difficult and he wished to continue his journey, 
he was not as solicitous as he should have been. 
But since God was managing matters better 
than Cortes could wish, although Cortes set 
forth from the port of Cozumel two or three 
times for New Spain he had to return on account 
of wild weather, and, realizing by this that God 
wanted those Christians to leave captivity and 
return to the service of God, he sent Diego de 
Ordaz and Martin de Escalante as captains of 
two brigantines and he sent a canoe to those 
Spaniards in the small vessel of the admiral’s 
ship, telling them that he had come there with 
eleven ships and for them to enter as best they 
could the small vessel, in guard of which he was 
sending two brigantines so that it might bring 
them more safely. These captains, suspecting 
that Aguilar might not know how to read very 
well, wrote another letter in a round hand with 
the same content as that of the general, adding 
that they would wait for them six days. They 
gave both letters to two Indians whom they had 
brought from the island of Cozumel, who, al- 
though with great fear, because they were at 
war with those of that coast, went inland. Our 
men waited for the reply the six days they had 
promised and two more besides. Meanwhile 
Cortes was troubled, believing either that the 
Spaniards were dead or that the Indians had not 
taken the letters; and so, the weather being very 
good, he decided to embark and continue his 
voyage. Setting out in fine weather, suddenly so 
great a tempest arose that all expected to perish 


woo 


and therefore it was necessary for them to return 
to the port for the third time. 

The Indians who took the letters, in order to 
give them secretly to Aguilar and the other Span- 
iards, put them in the roll of their hair, which 
they wore very long. They gave the letters to 
Aguilar who was very doubtful whether he should 
show them to the cacique, his lord, or whether 
he should go away with the messengers; and 
finally, both to preserve his honor and so that no 
danger might befall him, he went with them to 
his lord, and when he told him what they con- 
tained, the lord said to him, smiling: “‘Aguilar, 
Aguilar, you are very wise and you have well 
fulfilled what you owe to the love and fidelity 
which as a good servant you should have had, 
and you have done more than you thought be- 
cause I[ tell you that I had these letters in my 
hands before you did.’’ And it was so, for the 
Indians not only keep faith with their own lord 
but with another lord when they go to speak to 
him; and thus, these, secretly, although our men 
had given them orders to the contrary, went first 
to the lord. 

The lord having learned, then, what the letter 
contained, being astonished that the paper knew 
how to speak and that the absent conveyed their 
ideas by means of such small signs, because among 
the Indians, as of old the Egyptians (according 
to what Artemidorus writes), they did not make 
themselves understood by means of letters but 
by paintings; the lord, composing himself a 
little, for he had been angered by the news (be- 
cause, as we will relate below, Aguilar was very 
useful to him), said to him: “‘Aguilar, now what 
is it that you want to do now?” In reply to which 
Aguilar said, “Lord, only what you command.” 
The cacique, convinced of Aguilar’s submissive- 
ness, said to him again, “Do you want to go to 
your people?”’ Aguilar replied, “Lord, if you 
give me permission, I will go and I will return to 
serve you.” The cacique, with a more serene and 
joyful face, said to him, “Go in peace, then, al- 
though I know that you will not return again.” 
Nevertheless, he detained him for two days, wait- 
ing to see whether he would go or repent, and 


234 


when he saw that he did neither one thing nor 
the other, he summoned him and said, “Aguilar, 
great has been your goodness, your humility, 
fidelity and effort with which you have always 
served me in peace and in war. You are worthy of 
greater favors that I can do you, and although on 
the one hand the love I bear you and the need in 
which I must see myself, lacking your company, 
entice me; on the other, the same love, earned by 
your good services, and my duty as lord force 
me to give you liberty, which is the thing which 
the captive most desires; and since this is the 
greatest favor which I can do you, go in peace to 
your people; and I implore you by this good 
work which I do you and by others which I may 
have done for you to make me the friend of those 
Christians, inasmuch as I have learned from you 
that they are so valiant.” 
Having received this permission, Aguilar pros- 
trated himself at his feet with great humility, 
and with many tears in his eyes (I believe from 
excessive joy) said to him, “Lord, your gods be 
with you, for I will do what you command me 
me as I am obliged to do.”’ From there he went to 
take leave of the other Indian principales with 
whom he was friendly. They say that the cacique 
sent him to the coast accompanied by some In- 
dians and from there the Indians who had brought 
him the letters guided him. Going along the coast 
he learned that the brigantines had waited for 
him there a week and he found many crosses 
erected, kneeling before which, with many tears 
he worshipped and embraced them, for it seemed 
to him that he was already in a Christian land 
and that his long desire was fulfilled. And when 
he saw that the brigantines did not appear along 
the coast he was somewhat saddened, and, con- 
sidering what course he must take in order to 
attain his desire, going farther on, he saw the 
huts made of palms where our men had been, and, 
believing that they were within, he hastened his 
step with great joy, and when he arrived and 
found no one he was much dismayed. But since 
God was guiding him, going thoughtfully down 
the coast, when he had gone a league he stumbled 
upon a canoe full of sand which he emptied with 
the help of three Indians who accompanied him. 
The canoe had one side rotten which took water. 
Aguilar got in the canoe with them to see whether 
it could navigate and when he saw that it was 
taking too much water, making two of the In- 
dians jump ashore, he remained behind with one, 
leaning to the side where the water did not enter, 


APPENDIX D 


And when he saw that he could navigate in this 
way he went ashore to look for a stick with 
which to paddle. God provided that he found a 
stave of a cask with which he could paddle to his 
great satisfaction, and thus, going down the 
coast in search of the ships, crossing by the 
narrowest part, which would be about five 
leagues at least, he reached the coast of Cozumel; 
and on account of the great currents he touched 
two leagues from the ships. When he saw them, 
he jumped ashore with his companion and as 
they were going along the beach the next day, 
which was the first Sunday of Lent, after the 
general and his men had heard mass and were on 
the point of leaving again, a Spaniard named 
Angel Tintorero, who had gone out to hunt that 
morning in the bush, was gathering camotes, which 
is a fruit of the earth, when he raised his head 
and saw Aguilar coming, and, his heart telling 
him who he was, he said to him, ‘‘Brother, are 
you a Christian?” And when Aguilar replied 
that he was, without further delay Angel Tinto- 
rero replied, ‘“[hen I am going to ask the general 
for the reward for good news,”’ for he had ordered 
that a hundred pesos be given to the first man to 
bring him news of the Christian whom he so 
greatly desired to see. 

Angel Tintorero ran so fast, in order that no 
one else might win the reward for good news, 
telling those whom he met that Indian warriors 
were coming and in this way inducing them to 
return to the camp, that he reached the place 
where the general was almost without the power 
of speech. He asked him for the reward, and 
when it was granted, the joy with which he spoke 
was so great, that, almost beside himself, he 
sometimes addressed him as lordship and others 
as your grace. Finally, when he told what had 
happened to him as best he could and that Aguilar 
was coming, the joy which all the men received 
was so great that although Cortes had ordered 
under penalty that no one should go forth to see 
him, most of the army, one after another, set 
out by land, and almost all the sailors got into 
the boats to look for him by sea. And when the 
foremost who went by land met him, they gave 
many thanks to God, and embracing him, asked 
him diverse questions. Aguilar was so joyful that 
he could scarcely reply. Accompanied, then, by 
many people, he reached the general’s tent. He 
came stark naked except that his private parts 
were covered by a strip of cloth which the In- 
dians call mastil. His head was shorn from the 


CERVANTES DE SALAZAR 235 


forehead and sides to the crown, the remainder 
with very long black hair tied with cords, with a 
ribbon of red leather which reached below his 
waist. He carried a bow in his hand and a quiver 
with arrows hanging from his shoulder, and from 
the other shoulder a kind of purse made of net 
in which he carried his food, which was a kind 
of fruit they call camotes. He was so sunburned 
that he looked like an Indian except for his beard 
which he wore long, whereas the Indians of that 
land were accustomed to pluck it out with some 
things like pincers, as women do their eyebrows. 
He was all painted, which is done by smearing 
oneself with a certain bitumen which is red like 
ochre. This is useful against mosquitoes and 
against the heat of the sun. He was accompanied 
by the Indian of the canoe; others say, by the 
two Indians who took him the letters. 

And because I do not pretend to suppress other 
opinions, Motolinia, whom Gémara followed, 
writes that the first Sunday of Lent, when Cortes 
and his men had heard mass before leaving Cozu- 
mel, they came to tell him that a canoe was cross- 
ing and coming under sail from Yucatan toward 
the island and that it was coming directly toward 
the place where the ships were anchored; and 
that Cortes went out to see where it was going 
and when he saw that it was turning somewhat 
away from the fleet, he told Andres de Tapia to 
go secretly with some companions along the edge 
of the water to see whether those who were in 
the canoe went ashore. They did so. The canoe 
came ashore behind a point and four nude men 
got out. They wore their hair braided and tied 
on the forehead like women, and had their bows 
in their hands and quivers of arrows on their 
shoulders. Our men set upon them with bare 
swords in order to take them prisoners. Three of 
them, since they were Indians, fled. The other, 
who was Aguilar, stood still and in the language 
of the Indians told those who were fleeing not 
to be afraid, and, turning his face to our men, 
said to them in Castilian, ““Sefiores, are you Span- 
jards?’’ Others say that he said, “Sefiores, are 
you Christians?” They replied that they were 
and he rejoiced so greatly that he wept with 
pleasure, and, kneeling down at once, raising 
his hands to heaven gave many thanks to God for 
the grace he had done him in taking him from 
among infidels, where so many offenses were 
committed against God, and placing him among 
Christians. Andres de Tapia, cutting his speech 
short, going to him, embraced him lovingly and 


gave him his hand so that he might rise. The 
others also embraced him and thus he came with 
his Indian companions, talking to Andres de 
Tapia, telling him how he had been lost, until 
he reached the place where the Captain was. 


Cuaprer XXVI. How Aguilar reached the place where 
Cortes was and the manner in which he greeted him 
and was received. 


The desire which our people had to see Aguilar 
and to hear the strange things he had to tell was 
so great that some went up to high places, others 
came forward to take places where Cortes was, 
others went very near to him in order to enter 
together and hear what he might say. Aguilar 
having reached, then, the place where Cortes 
was, from a good distance away, with his head 
bowed he made a deep reverence. The Indians 
who came with him did the same, and then, draw- 
ing nearer, after having expressed to Cortes his 
pleasure at having come, he squatted with the 
Indians. All of them placed their bows and arrows 
on the ground on their right side, placing their 
right hands in their mouths, (and), having cov- 
ered them with saliva, they placed them on the 
ground and then brought them to the side of the 
heart, rubbing their hands. This was the manner 
of greatest reverence and respect with which 
those Indians venerated their princes, giving 
them to understand, according to my belief, that 
they prostrated and humiliated themselves before 
them like the earth they trod. 

Cortes, realizing that this was a ceremony and 
mode of salutation, again said to Aguilar that 
he was very welcome, because his coming had 
been greatly desired by him, and, taking off a 
long garment of yellow with crimson trimming, 
he threw it upon his shoulders with his own hands, 
asking him to arise from the ground and seat 
himself on a chair. He asked him his name and he 
replied Jeronimo de Aguilar and that he was a 
native of Ecija. Thereupon, Cortes asking him 
whether he was a relative of a gentleman named 
Marcos de Aguilar, he replied that he was. Hav- 
ing learned this, he continued by asking him if 
he knew how to read and write, and when he 
replied that he did, he asked him whether he 
had kept track of the year, month and day, and 
he told him exactly what it was, giving the 
dominical letter. Other things having been asked 
in this way, he ordered food to be brought to 
him. Aguilar ate and drank little. Asked why he 
ate and drank so temperately, he replied, like a 


236 APPENDIX D 


wise man, that it was because at the end of so 
long a time that he had been accustomed to the 
food of the Indians his stomach might refuse 
that of the Spaniards, and the quantity being 
small, although it were poison, it would do him 
no harm. They say that he was ordained by 
Gospel (ordenado de Evangelio) and that for this 
reason, as we will relate below, he never wished 
to marry. Cortes showed him many kindnesses 
and courtesies, realizing the need he had of his 
person in order to make the Indians understand 
that he was going to conquer; and since it would 
take too long to learn of the events of his life 
and how he had come to that state all at one time, 
he told him to amuse himself and rest until the 
next day, ordering the majordomo to clothe him. 
At the time [Aguilar] did not consider this a 
great favor, for he had so long been accustomed 
to go naked that he could not bear the clothing 
Cortes had put on him. 


Cuapter XXVIII. What Aguilar related the next day. 


On the next day, with no fewer people present, 
when Cortes asked him how he had come into 
the power of those Indians, he said, ‘‘Sefior, 
being involved in the wars of Darien and the 
passions between Diego de Nicuesa and Blasco 
Nitiiez de Balboa, | accompanied Valdivia, who 
was going to Santo Domingo to give an account 
of what was going on there to the admiral and 
governor and to [get] men and food as well as to 
bring twenty thousand ducats belonging to the 
king. This was in the year 1511. And when we 
had already reached Jamaica, the caravel was 
lost on the shoals they call those “‘of the vipers” 
or “‘of the scorpions” or “‘alligators.’’ With some 
difficulty twenty of us entered the small vessel, 
without sails and without bread or water and 
with a very poor equipment of oars.’’ Motolinia 
says this. Others who heard Aguilar say that 
those who entered the small vessel were only 
thirteen, of whom seven died within a short time 
because they came to such great extremity that 
they drank what they urinated. Six reached land, 
of whom four were sacrificed by the Indians. 
Two remained, who were Aguilar and a so-and- 
so de Morales. 
_ Continuing his discourse, Aguilar said: “And 
in this way we went on for fourteen days at the 
end of which the current, which is very strong 
there and always follows the sun, brought us 
to this land to a province called Maya. On the 
way seven of our men died of hunger, and the 


rest falling into the power of a cruel lord, he 
sacrificed Valdivia and four others, and, offering 
them to his idols, afterwards ate them, making a 
feast according to the custom of the country; and 
I, together with six others, remained in a coop, 
in order that for another festival that was ap- 
proaching, being fatter, we might solemnize their 
banquet with our flesh. Understanding that the end 
of our days was drawing near, we decided to 
venture our lives in another way, so we broke 
the cage in which we had been placed, and, flee- 
ing through the bush without being seen by a 
living person, God willed that although we went 
on with great fatigue, we should meet another 
cacique, an enemy of the one from whom we were 
fleeing. He was a humane and affable man, a 
friend of well-doing. He was called Ah-kin Cuz 
(Aquincuz), governor of Jamancona. He granted 
us our lives, although in exchange for great servi- 
tude in which he placed us. He died a few days 
later and I then served Taxmar, who succeeded 
him in the state. 

Five of my other companions died shortly 
thereafter on account of the miserable life they 
endured. I alone remained, and one Gonzalo 
Guerrero, sailor, who was with the cacique of 
Chetumal and married an important lady of that 
land by whom he has children. He is captain for a 
cacique named Nachancam and on account of hay- 
ing won many victories against the enemies of 
his lords he is greatly beloved and esteemed. | 
sent him your grace’s letter and asked him by the 
interpreter to come since the opportunity was so 
favorable, and I dallied waiting for him longer 
than I wished. He did not come and I believe 
from shame because he has his nostrils, lips, and 
ears pierced and his face painted (pintado) and 
his hands tattooed (/abradas) according to the 
custom of that country, in which only the valiant 
may have their hands tattooed. Indeed, I believe 
he failed to come on account of the vice he had 
committed with the woman and his love for his 
children. 

There are also others who say (which aston- 
ished the hearers not a little) that Aguilar said 
in this talk that when those who were still alive 
jumped out of the boat, they met Indians immedi- 
ately, one of whom split the head of one of our 
men, whose name he did not mention, with a 
macana, and that, pressing his head with both 
hands, he went into a thicket where he met a 
woman, who, pressing his head together, cured 
him, leaving a scar so deep that a hand could fit 


CERVANTES DE SALAZAR 2a) 


into it. He remained like a fool; he never wanted 
to be in a settled place, and by night he came for 
food to the houses of the Indians, who did him 
no harm because they had understood that their 
gods had cured him since it seemed to them that 
so frightful a wound could not be cured except 
by the hand of some one of their gods. They 
amused themselves with him because he was a 
fool (gracioso) and he lived unharmed in this life 
three years until he died. 

This discourse and tale inspired great wonder 
in those who heard it and every day both Cortes 
and his men asked him many other things which, 
because they are worthy of note and because of 
the pleasure of the story, I will set down in the 
following chapter. 


Cuapter XXVIII. Concerning the life lived by Aguilar 
with the lord whom he ultimately served and the things 
he did in his service. 


Those who were most intimate with Aguilar, 
whose story I continue in what I am going to 
tell, say that when he came into the power of 
this cacique, he made him serve him the first 
three years with great labor, because he made 
him bring wood, water, and fish on his back, and 
Aguilar bore these labors with a joyful face in 
order to assure life, which is so beloved. Natu- 
rally he was so submissive and obeyed with such 
humility that not only did he do with promptitude 
what his lord commanded him, but what any 
Indian, however humble he might be, to such an 
extent that although he was eating, if they ordered 
him to do anything, he left off eating in order to 
carry out the command. With this humility he 
won the heart and good will of his lord and of 
all those of his household and land. And because 
it is difficult to understand (?malo de conocer) the 
heart of man and the cacique was wise and desired 
to use Aguilar, as he did later on, in affairs of 
great consequence, seeing that he lived so chastely 
that he did not even raise his eyes to the women, 
he tried to tempt him many times, especially 
once when he sent him by night to fish in the sea, 
giving him as a companion a very beautiful Indian 
girl, fourteen years of age, who had been in- 
structed by the lord to provoke and attract 
Aguilar’s love. He gave her a hammock in which 
both might sleep. When they reached the coast, 
while they were waiting for the proper time to 
go fishing, which was just before dawn, hanging 
the hammock from two trees, the Indian girl lay 
down in it and called Aguilar in order that they 


might sleep together. He was so long-suffering, 
modest and temperate that, making a fire near 
the water, he lay down on the sand. The Indian 
girl sometimes called him, others told him he 
was not a man because he preferred to be in the 
cold to being embraced and warmed by her. He, 
although he was vacillating many times, finally 
determined to conquer his sensuality and fulfill 
what he had promised God, which was not to 
approach an infidel woman, in order that He 
might free him from the captivity in which he 
was. 

This temptation having been overcome and the 
fishing accomplished in the morning, he returned 
to his lord, who, in secret, before other principales, 
asked the Indian girl if Aguilar had approached 
her. When she told what had happened, from that 
time forward the lord held Aguilar in great es- 
teem, entrusting his wife and household to his 
care, from which it will easily be understood 
how virtue alone, even among barbarian peoples, 
ennobles men. Thenceforward Aguilar made 
himself loved and feared, because he had always 
carried out with prudence the things entrusted 
to him before he came into so great change of 
fortune. He said that on a feast day, the Indians, 
being painted with minium, were shooting with 
their bows and arrows at a dog they had hung 
from very high, when an Indian principal ap- 
proached Aguilar, who was watching it behind 
an enclosure of canes, and, seizing him by the 
arm, said to him: “Aguilar, what to you think 
of these archers, how accurate they are, for he 
who aims at the eye, hits the eye, and he who 
aims at the mouth, hits the mouth? Do you think, 
if you were placed there, that they would miss 
you?”’ Aguilar replied to him with great humility: 
“Lord, I am thy slave and you can do what you 
wish with me, but you are so good that you will 
not wish to lose a slave like me who will serve 
you so well in what you may command.” ‘The 
Indian afterwards told Aguilar that the cacique 
had sent him on purpose in order to learn, accord- 
ing to what they say, whether his heart was 


humble. 


Cuaprer XXIX. How Aguilar won certain battles in the 
service of his lord. 

Aguilar being in high favor with his lord, there 
occurred a war with another neighboring lord, 
which had been much disputed in years past and 
no one had been the victor; and thus, the hatreds 
between them enduring, as they usually do until 


blood is drunk, now that they were again at war, 
Aguilar said to him [his lord]: “Lord, | know 
chat you are in the right in this war and you know 
of me that I have served you with every care in 
all that has offered itself. | beg you to order given 
to me the arms which are necessary for this war, 
for | wish to employ my life in your service, and 
L hope in my God to come out with the victory.” 
The cacigue was much pleased and ordered to 
be given to him a shield and sabre (sacana), 
bow and arrows, with which he entered the battle, 
and since he fought with Spanish spirit, although 
he was not practiced in that kind of arms, in the 
presence of his lord he undertook many combats 
and won them fortunately. He distinguished him- 
self and displayed his prowess so much in the 
skirmishes that the enemies were already very 
much afraid of him and lost much of their spirit 
in the pitched battle which afterwards took place, 
in which Aguilar was the chief factor in his 
lord’s conquering and subjecting his enemies. 
This battle having been won, [and] the envy 
of Aguilar’s feats increasing among the neighbor- 
ing Indians, a very powerful cacique sent to tell 
his lord to sacrifice Aguilar immediately, for the 
gods were angry with him because he had con- 
quered with the aid of a man not belonging to 
their religion. The cacique replied that it was not 
right to give so bad a payment to one who had 
served him so well, and that Aguilar’s God must 
be good since he aided him so well in defending 
the right. This reply angered that lord so greatly 
that he came with a large force, determined to 
kill Aguilar by treachery and then to make his 
lord a slave; and thus, aided and favored by other 
neighboring lords, he came with a great force, 
sure that victory could not slip from his hands. 
When Aguilar’s lord heard this, he was very 
uncertain and even fearful of the outcome. He 
entered into council with the most important 
men. He summoned Aguilar to give his opinion; 
there were not lacking in the council some who, 
distrusting Aguilar, said that it was better to 
kill him than to fall into the hands of an enemy 
who came so powerfully. The lord harshly re- 
proved those who counselled this, and Aguilar 
arose with great spirit and said: “Lords, do not 
fear, for I hope i in my God, since you have justice 
on your side, that I will come out victorious; and 
it will be in this way, that at the time that the 
troops take position I will stretch out on the 
ground in the grass with some of your most 
valiant men, and then our army will pretend to 


APPENDIX D 


flee and our enemies will scatter and go carelessly 
with the joy of the victory and pursuit; and as 
soon as you have them at a distance from me, 
you will turn upon them with great spirit and 
then I will attack them from behind; and then 
when they see themselves heniumed in on both 
sides, however many they may be, they will be 
dismayed, because when enemies are perturbed, 
no matter how many they are, the more they are 
hampered. 

This advice greatly pleased the lord and all 
the others and they set forth at once to meet the 
enemy. Aguilar carried a shield and a Castilian 
sword in his hand and when they were in sight 
of the enemies, Aguilar, in a loud voice so that 
he could be heard by all, spoke after this fashion: 
“Lords, the enemies are near. Remember what 
was agreed, for today you are going to be slaves 
or lords of the whole land.” After he had said 
this, the troops engaged with a loud cry. Aguilar, 
together with some others, stretched out in some 
thickets, and the army began to flee and that of 
the enemies to follow them. Aguilar, when he 
saw it was time, attacked with such force that, 
killing and wounding, in a short time he wrought 
such great havoc that victory was soon known on 
his side, because those who went in the van, 
feigning to flee, regained such spirit and turned 
upon their enemies with such force that, killing 
many of them, they put the rest to flight. They 
took many principales prisoners, whom they after- 
wards sacrificed. With this victory Aguilar’s 
lord assured the safety of his land and state to 
such a degree that thenceforward there was no 
man who dared to attack him. This and other 
things which Aguilar did put him in such great 
favor with his lord that one day, being annoyed 
with a son of his, heir of the house and state, for, 
something, I know not what, that he said, he 
gave him a blow. The boy, weeping, complained 
to his father, who mildly told Aguilar that thence- 
forward he should be more careful what he did 
because if he did not have consideration for his 
good services, he would order him to be sacri- 
ficed. Aguilar replied with humility that the boy 
had given him cause and that he was sorry for it 
and that thenceforward he w ould not anger him. 
The lord, returning where his son was. ordered 
that he be whipped so that thenceforward he 
would not dare to make fun of older men than 
himself. Aguilar was confounded by this, al- 


though more favored and more greatly esteemed 
by all. 


CERVANTES DE SALAZAR 239 


After this, the ships of Francisco Hernandez >- 


de Cérdoba and those of Grijalva passed along 
that coast and because the Indians had some com- 
munication with them they esteemed Aguilar be- 
cause he was like the others, although they always 
kept him under careful surveillance so that he 
would not go away. 

They say, as Fray Toribio writes, that Agui- 
ar’s mother, when she knew that her son was in 


the power of Indians and that they ate human 
flesh, was so distressed that she went mad and 
never was willing to eat boiled or broiled meat 
thereafter, saying that it was her son’s flesh. And 
these and many other things are said of Aguilar, 
which I omit to write because they are not so 
well verified. And returning to the course of the 
history, I will tell something of the island of 
Cozumel and land of Yucatan.

CONCORDANCE 


In view of the many editions of Landa’s Rela- 
cién and the numerous references by page numbers 
to these various publications, there is presented 
here a Concordance, giving the folio and page 
numbers of the manuscript and the editions in re- 
lation to the present work. Throughout the book, 
the references to the editions are as follows: 


Tozzer, IT; the Landa manuscript, Ms; Brasseur 
de Bourbourg, BB; Rada y Delgada, RD; that in 
Relaciones de Yucatan, RY; Genet, G; Gates, 
WG; the Yucatecan edition of Rosado Escalante 
and Ontiveros, Y; and that of Perez Martinez, 
PM. The details of these editions can be found in 
the Bibliography.
